cues.say: Component nineteen: flags and kill switches.
A feature flag is a setting you flip while the site is running, with no code release. A kill switch is a flag for emergencies: it turns something off, fast.
Your app re-reads the flags every few seconds, from a database table or a config service. So a flip takes effect in seconds.
Why does that matter? Without a switch, changing what the site does means changing code. You write it, review it, test it and release it, in the middle of an incident.
That's twenty minutes or more of failed checkouts, at the worst possible moment.
A flag is just a named setting, like pause orders, stored outside your code. Every API copy reads it every few seconds.
The code checks it before it acts. If orders are paused, show a friendly message instead of the order button.
You flip it in an admin page. Seconds later, every copy has the new value, and the button changes. Orders that are already paid still finish.
A kill switch turns off an extra, like photos, so the core keeps working. That's called graceful degradation.
So install your switches before the event. Pause orders when payments fail. A waiting room when traffic is too much. Hide photos when the database is busy. Close a time slot when the ovens are full.
Now game day at the pizza shop. At four ten PM, payment errors spike.
Without a switch, someone writes, reviews and releases a fix mid-incident. Twenty minutes or more of failed checkouts.
With one, you flip pause new orders. Seconds later, the button says paused for a few minutes, and paid orders keep flowing.
At four twenty-five, payments recover, and you flip it back. Later, if the database gets busy, you flip hide photos.
Here's where it sits. The flags live in a small table, and every API copy reads them every few seconds.
Flipping one changes what the API does. Nothing is deployed.
Two things to know. Test every switch: one that nobody has flipped may not work when you need it. So flip each one on game day.
And clean them up after the event, because old flags pile up and make the code hard to follow.
In the interview, say: every switch is tested on game day.
